findings.where: Article specimen: the title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' and the closing paragraph's 'the world's best PPP law', at both widths
findings.fault: These apostrophes are straight typewriter marks. Elsewhere the same page sets curly ones: 'Mark’s' in the captions, '‘chapter topics’' in the subhead and '‘Abundance’' in the download link. The largest article heading on the sheet carries the wrong mark, and like marks are not set alike.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the development-bank readers the article is for. This tile's whole pitch is the polish of a legal journal, and a typewriter quote in a headline is the kind of slip a careful reader of legal text notices. It also tells Angélique nothing about which mark to use when she adds titles.

findings.where: First screen, at both widths: the hero line 'the story of public-private partnerships' and the supporting paragraph's 'Public-Private Partnerships' just below it. The same split recurs in the article: 'PPP Law' in the opening paragraphs, 'PPP law' in the subhead section and the close.
findings.fault: The same term changes capitalisation between the heading and the paragraph directly under it, and changes again within one article. The reader sees two spellings of Mark's central subject on a single screen.
findings.who_objects: A lawyer-advisor's audience, who are used to defined terms being capitalised the same way every time. On the first screen the mismatch makes the line and its supporting text look written separately rather than as one voice.
